Burgaw is Pender County's seat and one of its oldest small towns — a courthouse-square community of historic homes standing between the Holly Shelter Game Land's swamps to the east and the Northeast Cape Fear River to the west. That geography is the whole job: Burgaw is a town inside wetlands. Beaver work in the creeks and drainage around it, raccoons and bats in the tall attics of the historic stock, opossums and skunks under its porches, and a river-swamp mosquito economy that keeps every bat colony in the county fed. Burgaw.extendedBody:
Swamp-edge Burgaw: beavers, bats, and the drainage

Burgaw's ground calls are water calls. The creeks draining toward the Northeast Cape Fear, and the swamp systems toward Holly Shelter, put beavers within engineering distance of the town's low properties — dams that back water over drives and yards, girdled trees along the banks. Beaver work here is flow management as much as trapping: the dam, the culvert, and the water level are one system, and we treat them as one. In the historic homes, bats hold the attics — big browns in the tall roof voids — under North Carolina's calendar: no evictions during pup season, May 1 through July 31, with colonies found in the window mapped and excluded completely in August.

Licensed agents and depredation permits

Every operator we send to a Burgaw property is a licensed Wildlife Control Agent with the NC Wildlife Resources Commission. Removal work runs through the depredation permits the agent issues for your property — the legal instrument for the job, naming the species and the work. When you hire for wildlife work in North Carolina, that license and permit system is the credential to verify; it is also what obliges us to the state's handling rules for each species, rabies-vector animals included.

The historic-house read

On Burgaw's older homes we budget the inspection differently: the crawlspace and the attic both, the chimney from cap to cleanout, and every roof junction where an addition met the original house. The sealing that follows is metal and screen fitted to old framing — not foam, which squirrels treat as a door with a snack bar. Done once and done fully, it is the difference between a historic home that hosts animals and one that merely stands near them.

Rocky Point.extendedBody:
New subdivisions against the swamp

When a phase is graded, the raccoons, opossums, and armadillos that lived there move to the nearest cover — which is the finished street behind the clearing, its soffits, crawlspaces, and trash enclosures. Our subdivision work weights the boundary lots heaviest and treats 'nothing has been heard yet' as a reason for a perimeter inspection, not a clean bill: crawlspace vents, garage corners, and the lanai and porch junctions are where first-year entries happen. Sealing a new home on a boundary lot is the cheapest wildlife work in Pender County, because it is done before the first colony, not after.

The same system sets the bat calendar: North Carolina prohibits evictions during pup season, May 1 through July 31. River-side Rocky Point homes hold big brown bat colonies in their attics; colonies found in the window are mapped and staged, then excluded completely from August, with every gap sealed — a river attic left with one open gap is a colony again by the following spring.

River properties and the water pass
